hood Notes.
TEXAS.
Killed By a Train.
D. Wood of Greenville, Texas, was struck and instantly killed by a train at Berwyn, I. T., Monday night.

First Engineer Corps.

The first engineer corps of the state militia of Texas has been organized at Sherman. The militia is also to have a new adjutant, the appointment to be approved by the adjutant general.

Smallpox In Travlas County

A number of cases of smallpox have broken out on the lower border of Travis county, near Elgin. Rigid precautions will be taken to prevent the spread of the disease.

Burglars Make a Haul.

The hardware store of Halcomb and Miles at Luling, Texas, was robbed Saturday night of a large quantity of guns, revolvers, knifes, and ammunition, valued at more than $300.

Another Free Delivery

Four rural postal deliveries will be put into operation on September 1 at Alvarado. Texas. The four routes will reach 25000 people

Heavy Rains Ruin Roads.

The heavy rains recently in Bee county have made the roads almost impossible. The road improvement question is being strongly agitated again, with a prospect of some improvement in the matter.

To Dredge Texas Rivers.

Ool. C. S. Riche of Galveston has just returned to that city from St. Louis, where he had been on business in connection with the designing of a light draft dredge boat for use in the rivers of this state.

Largest Texas Broom Factory.

The largest broom factory in Texas was started last Wednesday at Round Rock. The machinery is of the latest pattern, and the concern is under the management of thoroughly trained business men. The industry will probably be a great success.
Race War Probable.

Great excitement has broken out in Sabine county, Texas, over the prospect of a race war between the whites and negroes. The blacks have posted notices threatening to kill three prominent citizens, and have been intimating women for some time past. Peace officers from adjoining counties have been asked for.

Drowned In Natatorium.

Ben Eddington, the sixteen year old son of N. D. Eddington of Temple, Texas, was drowned last Monday in the Temple natatorium pool. The boy who was unable to swim, reached for the swinging rings, missed his footing, and fell into the deep water. His friends attempted to rescue him but life was extinct when the body was found.

Proved To Be Gunpowder.

A small boy, a tin can, a match, and a handful of dust which proved on closer acquaintance to be gunpowder such as the Chinese invented, taught Gordon Templeton, the 11 years old son of Budge Templeton of Sherman, a lesseon in war fare which he will not forget. The boy was playing with the funny looking dust in the can when it suddenly exploded and burned the youngster about the face and shoulders.

Took Two Years To kill.

J. A. McKintosh, a farmer living four miles south of Gainesville Texas. has been looking for a negro for two years. Wednesday the negro returned to the county, and was shot and killed on sight. His name was Embry Thompson, and the offense which cost him his life occurred two years ago when he insulted the wife of Mr. McKintosh. McKintosh swore then to kill the negro whenever he saw him, and he kept his word. After the shooting McKintosh surrendered, and was immediately released on bond.

Ex-Gov. Hogg Leaves.

Former Governor Hogg will make democratic campaign speeches this year outside of Texas, at the earnest request of Chairman Jones of the democratic national committee. He will go to Chicago to speak for Bryanism. Governor Hogg is also a delegate to the American bar association which meets at Saratoga, N. Y., from August 29 to 31, and from there he will return to the Windy City for a conference with the democratic party managers. He will make speeches in Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Wisconsin, and New York. He will probably not return to Texas until after the campaign is closed.

The Original Alamo Bell.

The original Alamo bell has been turned over to the Daughters of the Republic of Texas at San Antonio, and will be hung in the Alamo with appropriate ceremonies. The bell was discovered three months ago at Goliad, where it was offered for sale as old iron by Moses Oppenheimer. The news of the discovery of the historic old bell was received at San Antonio with the result that it has been transferred to Miss De Zavalla, president of the Daughters. The bell is eighteen inches high, and weighs thirty-five pounds. On it is engraved the date 1772, and the words "San Antonio," together with the Spanish coat of arms.

John Davis, alias "Lamplighter," a negro, shot John Brennan, twenty years old, a white messenger boy, in the abdomen in front of No. 203 West Sixty-second-st., at 203 West Sixty-second-st. Brennan was taken to Roosevelt Hospital, and Dr. Brewer, the visiting physician, yesterday performed the operation of removing the bullet from the young man's stomach. Brennan's condition is critical. Directly traceable to this shooting were a number of race fights which broke out yesterday near the place where the boy was shot. Several of them gave promise of serious trouble, but the police suppressed them. A number of arrests were made.

Early yesterday morning James Arnold, a negro, fifty-five years old, of No. 220 West Sixty-fourth-st., was passing Sixty-fourth-st. and Amsterdam-ave. when a gang of white men attacked him. "Kill the black nigger!" one of the men shouted. Another declared the negro was the fugitive "Lamplighter," and nothing more was needed to excite the gang to a high pitch. They beat Arnold shamefully. A policeman finally arrived and drove the crowd away. Arnold seemed as much afraid of the policeman as of the mob, and declined to wait for an ambulance. An hour later he appeared at Roosevelt Hospital, where a surgeon put in half an hour dressing his wounds. Then he went home.

Almost a similar experience fell to Alexander Balentine, colored, thirty-two years old, of No. 218 West Sixty-second-st., as he passed Amsterdam-ave. at Sixty-second-st. He, too, was badly beaten, and was sent to Roosevelt Hospital. In neither case were arrests made.

The Rev. Len G. Broughton, of Georgia, in his sermon in the Hanson Place Baptist Church, in Brooklyn, last night, touched on the race riots in this city. He said:

When I read the account of that mob I said that this is enough to shut the mouth of every South hater in the North. In all the disgraceful riots in the South I never knew of one marked by the indiscriminate mobbing which you had. We ought to get this lesson from that mob—that the destruction of persons because of their color is the greatest crime which can be perpetrated against society. I stand as the champion of the colored man. I say that the colored man has the same right to enjoy every right under our flag that a white man has.

NEGROES SHOOT AND SLASH.
One White Man Shot in the Abdomen and Another Cut With a Razor.
There were several negroes standing at Sixty-second street and Amsterdam avenue at 11 o'clock on Saturday night. Most of them had just come out of a negro clubhouse at 203 West Sixty-second street. Among them was a young negro whose name is on the police records as John Davis. Nobody in the big negro colony above Fifty-ninth street ever calls him by that name, though, for he is known far and wide simply as "Lamplighter." He probably got the name from his height, which is about six feet and a half. "Lamplighter" has a police record. He is the reputed manager of a club for negroes and his face is scarred by razor slashes.

There was a group of young white men across the street from the negroes. A row started, and one of the negroes, said to be "Lamplighter," whipped out a revolver and fired five shots. One of the bullets struck John Brennan of 317 West Forty-seventh street in the abdomen and went through his body. Most of the participants in the row scattered. Brennan fell and became unconscious. He was taken to Roosevelt Hospital in a critical condition.

SOME INCIPIENT RACE RIOTS.
Bitter Feeling Again Breaks Out in New York.
New York, Aug. 26.—A number of incipient race riots between blacks and whites broke out here to-day, the direct cause being the shooting on Saturday night of John Brennan, a white messenger boy, aged twenty years, by John Davis, alias "Lamplighter," a negro. Brennan was one of a crowd of whites who taunted Davis, and bullets from the black's revolver fired at his tormentors lodged in Brennan's stomach and chest. He is in a hospital and likely to die. The shooting caused the rough white element to begin a search for negroes. Before daybreak this morning James Arnold, colored, while passing Sixty-fourth street and Amsterdam avenue, which is near the scene of the shooting, was attacked by a crowd of whites and shockingly beaten. He was treated at a hospital. Shortly afterwards, about two blocks away, a gang of whites administered similar punishment to Alexander Ballentine, a colored man, who was passing quietly along the thoroughfare. In neither case was an arrest made.

On New York Riots.
New York, Aug. 27.—The Rev. William Brooks, the colored pastor of St. Mark's M. E. church, preached a sermon to a large congregation last night on "The Story of the New York Riot." During the sermon the feelings of the congregation were at fever heat, and despite the pastors frequent admonitions to be calm, his hearers twice interrupted the sermon with vigorous applause. He said:

"I have been visiting the riot victims and making an investigation. I have a book of facts. What I say here tonight may send me before the courts, possibly to jail. In making the following charges against the police, I invite investigation :

"Innocent men were cruelly assaulted.

"The clubbing in nearly every case was done by the police.

"We have not found a single tough character among the victims maltreated, but honest, hard working persons.

THE NEW YORK RIOTS.
Sixteen New York Negroes, British subjects, injured in the recent New York riots, have appealed to the British council for redress. This puts a new and interesting aspect on riots in this country directed against our people, which will be worth watching. If the British government will, as it usually does, do its duty in this matter, it is going to have a salutary effect, both upon the American government and American mobs. Another element in the shape of Tammany hall's colored contingent has entered into the New York riots aftermath, which seems likely to cause considerable trouble for the police and police officials of the Empire city, who were either brutal in their treatment of Afro-Americans during the riot or permitted others to be so within their sight and hearing. E. Lee, the head of New York City's "united colored democracy," and a sort of a protege of Richard Croker, the leader of Tammany hall, headed a delegaton of Afro-Americans, members of his organization, who called upon acting Mayor Guggenheimer (also a creature of Mr. Croker's) and protested against the course of the police in the recent disturbances. "There was no race viot," said Mr. Lee. "Negroes were attacked and instead of receiving protection from the police, they were brutally treated by them. The police paid no attention to white men, but appeared to be glad of the opportunity to club Negroes. There were very few Negroes hurt by white men compared to those that were injured by policemen's clubs when they had committed no offense and were only trying to protect their lives. The Negroes are incensed at the action of the police and we want an investigation." When it is remembered that Mr. Lee is at the head of an organization, started at the instance of Mr. Richard Croker, the real head of Greater New York, and Mr. Lee's position as stated above is understood, it will be seen that there is trouble ahead for certain New York City policemen, because Mr. Croker and Tammany hall are extremely anxious to increase this fall the organization's colored membership, which is already very large, because of the large number of political positions given by him to Afro-Americans of that city. Indeed, Tammany hall's claim that it has given to Afro-Americans of New York City as many and as good positions as the present national republican administration has given to
which is already very large, because of the large number of political positions given by him to Afro-Americans of that city. Indeed, Tammany hall's claim that it has given to Afro-Americans of New York City as many and as good positions as the present national republican administration has given to all of the Afro-Americans of the entire north, has thus far gone unquestioned. As a result of Mr. Lee's calling upon the acting mayor and the latter's communications to the police commissioners of the Empire city, as well as the protests of various race organizations, it has been decided by the police commissioners to take action in regard to the complaints of brutality on the part of policemen during the recent riots on the West Side of New York City. One of the fairest persons to deal with any phase of the riots in question was Magistrate Cornell, of this city, whose talk, decisions and warning to the police indicate a breadth of mind, fairness and ability most encouraging indeed. He put a stop to the New York police's dragging Afro-Americans indiscriminately into his court room and warned the police that they "ought to arrest more whites to do justice in the riot." His warning was productive of much good; it was heeded. These riots, as well as all others directed against our people, are but giving vent to an additional latent prejudice which exists in every community of this country and which eagerly grasps every opportunity to show its hydra head. The spread of mob violence throughout the north during the last three or four weeks has been unprecedented and ought to call the government's attention to the spread of the disease and secure for it the attention it is entitled to, because of the dangerousness from a governmental standpoint of its character. The policeman whose death at the hands of an Afro-American was the cause of the New York riots had so demeaned himself as to bring about just such a result. His treatment of the colored people in his vicinity was such as to secure for him the enmity of the entire Afro-American population of that neighborhood. His death enraged the police and furnished the opportunity for venting a latent prejudice, upon the part of hundreds of prejudiced whites.

H. H. Hackett of Princeton Was Defeated at Tennis. Nlagara-on-the-Lake, Ontario, Aug. 27.—R. D. Little of Princeton retained his title as champion in the international tennis tournament here to-day. His opponent was H. H. Hackett of Princeton, who was beaten in a four-set match. The ladies' handcap singles was also finished, and the tournament will conclude to-morrow with the men's handicap finals. WOMAN'S PERILOUS TRIP. Narrowly Escaped Death Searching for Her Husband.
Seattle, Wash., Aug. 27.—A thrilling trip down the Koyukuk River recently fell to the lot of Mrs. Hewitt, wife of a Chicago physician, now at Nome. Alone and lost for months in a dreary waste, she managed to reach the Yukon River on a log raft. There she was rescued by the river steamer Hannah, picked up and sent to Nome to her husband.

Mrs. Hewitt left Chicago two years ago to join her husband. He was located at St. Michael at first, but afterward went to Nome. Late in the fall she started over to Dawson with a party. When they reached Fort Hamilton she heard of rich strikes at the headwaters of the Koyukuk and started across country to join the rush for that place.

After reaching the Koyukuk, Mrs. Hewitt became lost on a branch of the river. With her dog team, she made frantic efforts to get back to camp, but only succeeded in further bewildering herself. Finally she was compelled to camp at a deserted Indian hunt. The party she was with made efforts to find her, but did not succeed in doing so and about the first of June, the river breaking up, she constructed a log raft and floated down 750 miles to Yukon.

DEAD, SITTING UPRIGHT.

William Durkin, a Negro, Found on a Doorstep.

A negro, supposed to be William Durkin, was found dead on the doorstep in front of a house at the northeast corner of Jefferson avenue and Market street about 11:30 o'clock last night.

When found, he was sitting upright on the steps, with his back resting against the door. It is thought that the negro sat down to rest and died from heart disease. An ambulance was summoned by the policeman that found him, and, as he was not sure that the man was dead, he had him sent to the City Dispensary. Doctor Voerster pronounced life extinct, and the body was sent to the morgue.

Doctor Voerster said that the man had not been dead long. There were no traces of poison. In the negro's pocket was found a notebook, on the fly-leaf of which was inscribed: "My name is William Durkin." No other marks of identification were found on the body.

GIRLS' PROTECTOR KILLED.

Aged Iowa Negro Defended Young Women Against Tramps.

Marshalltown, Ia., Aug. 27.—Four tramps insulted two young girls in the outskirts of town this evening. An old negro drayman named Williams went to the rescue of the girls, when two of the tramps shot him to death with revolvers.

A posse is in pursuit of the murderers. The entire negro population is aroused, and if the murderers are caught they may be lynched.

Williams was an inoffensive citizen and leaves a family.
joseph-williams-marshalltown-1900-08-27.A4:
Joseph Williams, a highly respected colored man of this city, has reversed the usual order of things, and has sacrificed his life in what he considered an effort to protect the persons and the honor of two white girls who were in the clutches of a gang of drunken tramps in the southeastern part of the city. Williams, after rescuing the girls, was foully murdered within a few blocks of his own home, while making an effort to notify the police and secure the arrest of the tramps—was shot to death with his own revolver, it is supposed, which had fallen into the hands of one of his assailants, who is now supposed to be in custody.

The crime is somewhat similar to that occurring just one year ago on the 22d inst., when tramps committed a shocking double murder by shooting Brakemen Wilson and Matthews while in the discharge of their duty, and no tragedy since then has so stirred the indignation of the populace as that of Monday evening.

When word reached the business part of the city from the southeastern district that Williams had been murdered by tramps, the news spread like wild fire, and the officers, leaving in haste for the scene, were followed by many who were not aware of the circumstances, yet followed to see "what was up." Especially in the south part of the city was the excitement intense, many leaving their evening meals to go to the vicinity of the Marshalltown Canning Company's plant, near where the murder was committed.

STORY OF THE CRIME.

Joseph Williams, the murdered man, is a familiar figure on the streets, and will be recalled by many who did not know his name as being a nice appearing colored man, who drove a single horse dray, doing a business in that line on a small scale. About 6 o'clock Monday evening he was returning from up town to his home on Ketchum street, between Tenth and Eleventh avenues, taking his usual route by the west side of the canning factory. As he passed the corner of the Northwestern stock yards, which are a short distance to the south and west, he noticed two little girls, Rosa Buhrer, aged 15, daughter of William Buhrer, of 910 South Center street, and Mary Khile, aged 12, daughter of John Khile, of 911 South Center, crying. Near them, and surrounding them, were a gang of eight or ten tramps, who were reveling over a keg of beer. The men had been drinking considerably. Williams supposed they had intercepted the girls as they were on their way home for supper from the canning factory, where they are employed as huskers. He went to the girls' assistance, as did also James Clem, another drayman, who had been over on the south side delivering a trunk. The hobos, who outnumbered the rescuers three to one, gave them warning that they had better not interfere, calling each of the men names as they spoke. Seeing that it was of no use to try to use force with the men, but having accomplished their purpose of allowing the girls to pass by undisturbed, they went their ways. After the shooting began there were several eye witnesses to the tragedy. The first shot attracted the attention of John Raber, formerly proprietor of the Globe hotel, but now an employee of the canning company. Raber was in the part of the building nearest the scene and upon looking up when he heard the shot saw Williams running towards the factory, with four men close at his heels. The man doing the shooting was slightly in the lead of the others. Two more shots were sent after the fleeing negro, but they missed him, and by that time the man with the gun had reached a point within six or eight feet of the colored man. He stopped for a moment, raised the smoking weapon again, and Williams, having tripped and fallen, begged him not to shoot again. The tramp did not heed his pleadings, however, and with truer aim this time, set another ball from the 38-caliber revolver, striking the colored man directly over the right kidney. Williams still managed to stumble along, aiding his steps by grasping the edge of the canning factory platform, from which the cars are loaded. Raber was very near him and heard Williams' moans, and his cries of "Oh, God, I am shot." Raber asked him how many times he had been hit and, the man answered, "Only once."

Altho bleeding from the wound Williams was able to walk to the canning factory office, where he was made as comfortable as possible. The man who shot him turned leisurely about, walked back to the place where a few moments before he was drinking beer with his companions, and, as cool as could be, drew another can of beer from the keg. He also broke the revolver and emptied the four exploded cartridges to the ground.

Altho Williams did not indicate by his suffering that he was dangerously wounded, he lived but fifteen minutes, lapsed into unconsciousness shortly af-
joseph-williams-marshalltown-1900-08-27.A7:
year-old boy who was at the scene, is also positive Gray in the man.

Polly Kendall, Octavia Streeter and Fay Hazen, three girls who are employed at the candy factory, but who had gone, after their day's work, to view the operations of the canning establishment, saw Williams running, saw the big man in the lead of the four after him, and saw the fatal shot fired after Williams had fallen. They were taken to the jail to inspect Gray and are quite certain, but not absolutely positive that he is the one. In their opinion the three men with Gray were trying to prevent him from shooting the colored man.

Another of the suspects under arrest has been positively identified by Mr. Clem and by the Buhrer and Khile girls as one who was sitting on the beer keg when the trouble commenced. He is a typical hobo, not very intelligent, is not as vicious appearing as Gray, and at the time was considerably under the influence of liquor. This fellow was arrested by Deputy Sheriff McFarland, Clyde Morse and Coroner Lierle in the southwestern part of town and while attempting to board a Great Western freight. He resisted arrest, but was overpowered.

THE TWO GIRLS' STORY.

From the story told by the Buhrer and Khile girls and Miss Streeter it is certain that Williams misunderstood the situation and that misunderstanding cost him his life. Misses Buhrer and Khile says 'that two colored girls who are larger than they and who are employed at the cannery had been abusing them, and that one, after they left the factory, slapped Rosa Buhrer in the face. For this act the tramps, including Gray, interfered in behalf of the white girls, and before Williams and Clem arrived the colored girls had disappeared from the scene. The interference of the tramps in the smaller girls' behalf is the only extenuating circumstance on their part in the whole affair. Williams, however, from his dying statement made to several, including Miss Streeter, was under the impression that the tramps had insulted the white girls. Miss Streeter says when Williams went past her on his way to the cannery office he exclaimed: "They have done it! They have done it!" adding that they had insulted the white girls and that he resented it. Whether they did so or not the girls do not say, but owing to their youth they may not have understood the proposals of the tramps.

John Raber was also brought up to identify Gray, but he was not able to say positively that he was the man. A third one of the prisoners, whose name has not been learned, he was able to identify as one of the crowd. This man admits the fact that he was among the beer drinking party, and is inclined to tell the whole story. He says five of the men started to Tama on a freight train, and word from that place says that number of suspects were taken from a train by the officers there and are being held. Sheriff Shoemaker went to Tama at noon to secure the men and return them to the city. It looks now as if the whole facts will be known and just punishment meted out to the one guilty of the foul crime. It is time an example was being made of this class of toughs, who are too ready to murder without provocation.

Forty of the colored men of the city organized and assisted in the search during the night.

THE MURDERED MAN.

Joseph Williams, the murdered man, had been a resident of Marshalltown for ten years. He was 49 years of age and leaves a wife and six children—three sons and three daughters. All of the children are at home excepting the eldest daughter, Mrs. George Dixon, who lives in Rockford, Ill. The modest little home on Ketchum street was a pretty sad place when visited by a T.-R. man shortly after the murder. Mrs. Williams was nearly prostrated and the children were lying here and there, weeping over the loss of their father. A circumstance that makes the affair all the more sad at the present time is the fact that Mrs. Williams is soon to become a mother. Mr. Williams was one of the better class of colored people of the city, and was a hardworking, industrious man. He was known among his neighbors, both whites and blacks, as an inoffensive man and one who was in the habit of attending to his own affairs and letting others alone. He is a member of the Colored Odd Fellows' lodge, of this city.

After Williams died and Coroner Lierle arrived to look over the ground and investigate the circumstances, the remains were taken to the parlor of H. E. Simkins, where they were prepared for burial.

Arrangements have not been perfected by Coroner Lierle for the inquest, but it will probably be held Wednesday, as will the funeral of Mr. Williams.

TO SATISFY JUDGMENT.
joseph-williams-marshalltown-1900-08-27.A8:
LOOKS BAD FOR GRAY

Not Much Doubt But That the Wil-
liams Murder Will Be Charged
to Him.

Several Witnesses Tell the Coroner's
Jury He Was the Man Who
Fired the Shots.

A Pal Attempting to Fix the Crime
on Another—The Coroner's
Inquest.
It appears quite certain that the murder of the colored man, Joseph Williams, will be charged against the suspect who says his name is Gray and that he will have to answer to the courts for the offense. With several reliable men swearing positively that he is the one who fired the several shots at Williams, and the testimony of one of the other tramps under arrest that Gray was of the party, will make a strong case against him, altho this third man is attempting to shield Gray and fasten the responsibility for the colored man's death on another whose name he claims he does not know.

The third man arrested is the one referred to Tuesday as doing considerable talking. He gives his name as Dunn, and is a large man like Gray, but wears a sandy mustache and has a florid complexion, while Gray is dark and is smoothe shaven. Dunn at first denied strenuously that he was in the party, but when confronted by Sheriff Shoemaker and John Raber with the details of his actions at that time he admitted that he was in the crowd. Raber, who witnessed the shooting, says Dunn was among the three who followed closely on the heels of the man who killed Williams and was after met by Raber near the stock yards and emerging from behind some buildings and lumber piles. Dunn is, in the opinion of the officers, trying to shield Gray, and that the man who had the revolver was a tall fellow with a sandy mustache whose name he does not know. This in a way is a description of the second of the suspects identified as among the party—the one who was sitting on the beer keg during the quarrel and considerably intoxicated.

Coroner Lierle this morning empaneced a jury and commenced the inquest, which has occupied most of the day. The jury selected was L. C. Abbott, Theodore Johnston and C. C. St. Clair—all excellent men. The proceedings were conducted in the sheriff's office and County Attorney Stone assisted in the examination of the witnesses. Dr. Mighell testified concerning the nature of the fatal wound, etc. Lewis Cleveland, a cannery employee who saw the men holding Williams and heard the shots, also testified, and said the man with the revolver was the one who gives his name as Gray, John Raber, another cannery employee and who was, probably, nearer to the scene than any of the others who witnessed the tragedy, gave the details about as outlined in these columns heretofore. He with George B. Hayes, testified that Williams, after he was hit, said the tramps had insulted the girls and he had resented it. Raber also said that when Williams was shot Gray, or a man answering his description, was within a few feet of the victim, and when he fell three other tramps surrounded him.

The clothing worn by the murdered man at the time was exhibited, and an examination shows that one of the first shots went thru one of the pantaloon legs and grazed the leg of the colored man.

Pat Dunn, one of the tramps under arrest, was put on the stand this afternoon to tell what he knew of the affair. Dunn told a confusing and conflicting story, trying first to clear himself of any participation in the affair, and second, to fasten the crime on some one not under arrest. He declared that he was drunk and lying by the stockyards fence all the time; that he was too drunk to participate, but that he knew Gray was not the one, saying that the man who did the shooting, with two companions, boarded a freight train immediately after and started towards Tama. He said further that Gray was not in the crowd at the time, but that he met him later near by. This is in direct contradiction to the statement he made to Sheriff Shoemaker and John Raber Tuesday, when he said that Gray was one of the party. Dunn disgusted the jury by his conflicting statements and was taken back to jail.

George Spencer, a cannery employee; Frank Solomon, an eye-witness to the tragedy; John Stepan and others were examined, the investigation not being concluded until this evening.

The jury will probably declare that Williams was killed by one of a number of tramps and may recommend that Gray and Dunn be held, but will probably not say definitely who, in t heir opinion, committed the murder, leaving that for the courts to say.

The five men arrested at Tama and brought to the city could not be identified as being among the party, altho three of them admitted they were with the crowd prior to the trouble.

A TRAMP'S BOLDNESS.
joseph-williams-marshalltown-1900-08-27.A11:
JURY'S VERDICT SEALED
Findings of the Coroner's Jury in the Williams Murder Not Made Public.
Gray and Dunn Will Be Held to the Grand Jury, Which Convenes Next Week.
Witnesses Testify That Both Had Revolvers and Two Say Dunn Did the Shooting.
The coroner's investigations of the murder of Joseph Williams, the colored man, were concluded at 5:30 o'clock Wednesday evening, but it was decided by the jury to return a sealed verdict and this will not be made public until after the grand jury convenes, next week. Gray, Pat Dunn and the tramp umbrella mender who was at the scene of the murder are being held, however, the two first named as accomplices in the crime and the latter as a witness.

The jury and coroner concluded to keep the findings of the jury secret for the present for several reasons. One is owing to the intense feeling of the people and quiet threats that are being made to lynch the murderer. Another is because the jury desired a fair and impartial investigation on the part of the grand jury and did not wish its verdict to have any effect on the probable actions of the court jury. It is presumed, however, that the coroner's jury deemed the evidence sufficient to warrant the holding of both Gray and Dunn, especially as the latter has told conflicting stories in an apparent effort to clear both himself and Gray, and as witnesses have identified both Gray and Dunn as the man who did the shooting.

Before the inquest was concluded eight of the witnesses and the jury visited the county jail. A number of the tramps arrested on suspicion were ranged in a row and the witnesses asked to pick out the man who fired the fatal shot. Six named the man known as Gray, while two identified Dunn as the one. The two prisoners are both large and built much the same, both wear soft, round hats very much alike, but Gray is taller, is smooth faced except for a week's growth of beard, while Dunn is of florid complexion and has a sandy mustache. A majority of the witnesses insist that the man who did the shooting wore a black shirt, and this is what Gray is wearing.

It is not improbable that two of the tramps had revolvers and that both fired their weapons at the colored man. On this point the evidence before the coroner was somewhat conflicting. Charles Stepan, who witnessed the shooting, testified that both Gray and Dunn had revolvers in their hands, but that Gray did the shooting. Frank Solomon saw the fatal shot fired and identified Dunn as the man who did it. Dr. Mighell's evidence also shows there is some conflict as to the facts, and that if Williams had a revolver prior to the shooting it was not the one from which the fatal shot was fired. Dr. Mighell said the bullet he extracted from the wound was from a center fire cartridge, while the cartridges found in Williams' home were of the rim fire variety. Whether or not these discrepancies in the testimony will have an effect on the final outcome of the case, or whether Dunn or Gray or both can be proven as responsible for the colored man's death remains to be seen.

The old umbrella mender is known to be conversant with the circumstances, and may be compelled, to clear himself of complicity, to divulge the facts and tell which of the prisoners, if either, fired the fatal shot.

A total of forty-nine prisoners were in the county jail Wednesday night, but a dozen or more of the tramps arrested on the night of the murder and held since then were discharged this morning, owing to the outcome of the coroner's investigations.
joseph-williams-marshalltown-1900-08-27.A12:
NEGRO DRAYMAN KILLED.
Shot by Three Tramps in Sight of Speetators at Marshallitown.
Marshalltown, Aug. 28.—Joseph Williams, a negro drayman, was murdered last evening at 6 o'clock by three tramps on the railroad at the side of Marshall Canning Company's factory within view of many employes. The murderers had hold of the negro and shot him in the back and then ran. The men had been drinking, but it is yet unknown how Williams came to be with them. He was probably on his way home. The men employed in the factory were evidently too scared to take action and awaited the officers.

The authorities at Marshalltown notified Sheriff Cricket of the murder last evening. It was stated that the colored man was not in company with the tramps, but that he was passing them. The tramps had been "rushing the can" all day and were thought to be quite a little intoxicated. Three bullets were sent into the body of the colored man and he died instantly.

Only imperfect descriptions of the man who did the shooting could be obtained and it is a mere chance if the tramps are caught. The fellows had little difficulty in making their escape before the officers could get to the scene of the murder.

Unfortunate Woman Released
Fort Dodge, Aug. 30.-The grand jury during its session thoroughly investigated the case of Jane McIntyre, the woman found in the weeds near the Des Moines river bank with a new born babe by her side, which had died from exposure. She was not sufficiently insane to be made an inmate of the asylum, and yet, the judge held, her mind was not strong enough to receive the empathy of the offense which she had committed.

Murderer Identified

Marshalltown, August 29.—Among the thirty-five tramps arrested and now in the county jail here, one named Gray has been positively identified as the man who killed Joseph Williams, the colored drayman, who defended two young girls from assaults by a gang of tramps last evening; Gray is strongly guarded, and ally though excitement is still intense among the negroes, violence will not be attempted.

Farmer Fentally Hurt

Grimmel, Aug. 29.—John Basby, a stock farmer of New Sharon, while getting on a moving train with stock on the Iowa Central here, was caught, under the wheels and had both legs cut off above the knees. He died in two hours from loss of oxygen, but he only would feel Two of his sons were killed by lightning two years ago in the presence of himself and wife.

Pecullar Verdict In Inguest:

Fort Dodge, Aug. 29. - The sudden and suspicious death of a laboring man named John G. Angquist caused the coroner, Dr. H. Rose, to hold an inquest over the remains. The jury returned a verdict that the man had died from blood poisoning, caused by a scratch in his foot which he received five years ago. The claim was that the blood poisoning was chronic.

LOCAL COMMENT.
When the water extension is completed and proven to be successful Marshalltown citizens ought to combine in one great and grand jollification. This would be the most effective means of publishing to the whole state that we have the most important necessity of a growing and prosperous city—a pure water supply.

The Marshall county jail never contained a larger or harder lot of criminals than it does at the present time, and the grand jury has a big grist to grind. Murray, one of the State Center safe crackers, is among the jolliest of the big bunch awaiting trial, and recently remarked, when another prisoner was brought in, that Marshall county would be compelled to run a special excursion train to Fort Madison for their special benefit. Murray, used an expression new here, and, when asking how long it would be before the court would dispose of his case, remarked that the quicker the better, so he could be "hittin' the grit," meaning that he desired to commence the serving of his sentence as soon as possible instead of wasting time in the county jail.

Some means ought to be found of restricting the sales of liquor to the hobo element that has infested this city during the past two years. While the extensive railroad improvements been in progress in this vicinity this community has been overrun with a vicious element. The railway company is not to blame, as enough good and steady men can not be procured and every one is hired who comes along and shows a disposition to work. This condition has caused an unusual number of tramps and toughs to come this way. They work a few days or a week, come to town and with companions invest in several kegs of beer and then raise all kinds of disturbance. The vacant space near the stockyards has been a favorite rendezvous and the scene of drunken revelry almost daily during the past summer. If the police rounded them up or drove them away, there would be
the revelry almost daily during the past summer. If the police rounded them up or drove them away, there would be others to take their places. It would require a whole company of soldiers to properly police that section of the city and keep it free from drunken tramps and drunken crooks, who, under the guise of tramps, steal and rob, and murder if they find it more convenient to do so. The only means at hand to cause this class to give Marshalitown the go-by is to prevent the wholesale of liquors to them. This may not be an easy matter to do, but since the murder of the colored man last Monday Mayor Pierce has taken the matter up and may find some means of bringing about this result. While a hobo's money, in the opinion of most saloonists, is as good as any other man's money, the self-respecting liquor dealer ought to hesitate in making sales in large quantities until he knows where and to whom the liquor is going. The dealer could be prosecuted under the habitual drunk section of the mulct law, as a majority of these tramps and crooks are habituals because they get drunk every time they get the opportunity or a little money. If the mayor will take the bull by the horns he will have the moral backing of nearly every citizen of Marshalltown. Another crime like that of a few days ago might make a lynching impossible to prevent, and Marshalltown doesn't desire the free advertising such a regrettible incident would be sure to bring.

A druggist who resides on East Main street has lost his reputation as a cow fancier, and his friends now declare that he doesn't know a cow from a horse. They think he would claim as his own any old cow. The other day the source of the household milk supply got loose and strayed away. The owner set out to find her and was gone some time. During his absence a man of whom he had made inquiries appeared at the kitchen door leading a bovine and reported that he had found the lost animal. The druggist's wife told him to tie the cow in the barn and gave him a quarter for his trouble. Soon the owner returned from his unsuccessful search and was pleased to find that her Jerseyship was safe and sound. Desiring to send the cow away for the day, he employed a colored man to take charge of her and instructed him to stay close to her all day long and he would be justly rewarded. The T.-R. regrets to tgll the balance of the story, but is called upon to do so. In the evening the druggist was surprised to see his Jersey walk leisurely into the yard, unaccompanied and satisfied with her day's grazing in the pasture, and not until then did it dawn upon him that he had hired the colored man to take charge of the property of some one else and had paid a quarter to a man for bringing him a cow that he had no claim to. He is now considering the advisability of buying milk from a dairyman, as he says keeping a cow in town has its disadvantages as well as its advantages.

A citizen has called the attention of the T.-R. to the fact that while our town possesses a commercial club there has been little effective work done to increase the town's employing institutions and said citizen wants the T.-R. to "roast" the club. Upon discussing the question with the citizen he amended his suggestion to read that the T.-R. "roast" the method on which our commercial club is trying to do business and he proceeded to make some very sensible criticisms. He cited the axiom that what is everybody's business becomes nobody's business and that to this fact more than any other was due the present inactivity of our commercial club. He thought that instead of the club as a body trying to at-
joseph-williams-marshalltown-1900-08-27.A24:
JUST AN EVEN DOZEN
That Number of Prisoners Indisted by the Grand Jury and Arraigned.
Both Gray and Dunn Charged With the Murder of Joseph Williams; Colored.
McCabe, Murray, Russie, Seino, Harris, Hesser, Block and Others In the List.
The grand jury concluded its deliberations this afternoon and shortly after 2 o'clock reported its findings to the court. Twelve of the prisoners in the county jail were indicted for various offenses, and it is thought that several other bills were returned against men not under arrest. Among the indicted are John Gray and Pat Dunn, who are accused of the murder of Joseph Williams, the colored teamster. The list of those indicted, as far as made public, follows:
John Gray, murder.
Pat Dunn, murder.
J. H. McCabe, safe blowing and burglary, two indictments.
T. J. Murray, same offense, two indictments.
F. D. Russie, rape, two indictments.
Pearl Harris, cheating by false pretenses.
Haskell Judy, breaking and entering.
Joe Hesser, breaking and entering.
Ed Block, breaking and entering.
Joe Seino, assault with intent to commit murder.
Henry Haskell, larceny from a building in the night time.
James Wren, same offense.
The twelve prisoners were immediately arraigned, were given counsel if they had not already employed the same, and were offered the opportunity to plead. Gray and Dunn took time to plead. The latter said his home was in Albert Lea and the former said he came from Chicago. Murray and McCabe, the State Center safe crackers, took time to plead, as did also Pearl Harris, the colored man who forged an order on J. H. Sundell. Haskell Judy, who is charged with entering a farm house, plead not guilty. Seino, the Italian who engaged in a duel with Joe Rio, entered a similar plea, as did Hesser and Block, the men accused of breaking into a Great Western car and stealing therefrom a quantity of goods.
Haskell and Wren, who were arrested at Gilman a few nights ago for stealing goods from the H. A. Church store and who were indicted for larceny from a store in the night time, said they did not care to have counsel appointed and entered pleas of guilty. The maximum penalty for this offense is one year in the county jail.

An effort was made to have George Doolittle indicted for the assault on A. W. Heald, but no bill was returned. In appointingg counsel for those who had not employed such, Judge Caswell served notice that he would not select any one who had gone to the jail to solicit business.

The Myers-Northwestern case was adjourned at noon until Monday and will probably occupy several days next week. It is developing into an interesting controversy, entailing as it does several new points relative to condemnation proceedings where lands are desired.

louis-gibson-augusta-1900-08-27.A1:
SUSTAINED THE POLICEMAN.
Coroner's Jury Exonerated Belding. S. M. Whitney of Augusta Dead.
Augusta, Ga., Aug. 26.—The coroner's jury to-day returned a verdict of justifiable homicide in the case of Policeman W. M. Belding, who shot the negro, Louis Gibson, last night, who resisted arrest and had seized the policeman's club and assaulted the officer. Gibson was heating his wife, and when the officer responded to the woman's cries Gibson would not submit to arrest, but was engaged in a terrible struggle with the policeman when the latter shot and killed him.

Mr. S. M. Whitney, one of Augusta's best known cotton factors, died to-day in Lynn, Mass., where he was on a visit to two of his sons, who are graduates of the technological Institute and hold important positions in Lynn. Since the murder of his son, Alexander Whitney, on the street car about three months ago, Mr. Whitney has been much depressed, but his death was not anticipated, and the news was a shock to his family and friends here.

Mr. Whitney was born in New York in 1829 and came to Elberton, Ga., in 1853. After the war he came to Augusta, and in 1869 married Miss Sallie Berry of Atlanta. For many years he was a successful cotton factor in Augusta and an authority on Cotton Row. He is survived by his wife, two brothers, two sisters and five sons. His remains will reach Augusta on Tuesday.
louis-gibson-augusta-1900-08-27.A2:
POLICEMAN KILLS A NEGRO.
Officer Sends a Bullet Through Desperado's Brain.
perado's Brain.
AUGUSTA, Ga., Aug. 27.—Louis Gibson, a desperate negro character, was shot and instantly killed by Policman William M. Belding. The officer heard cries coming from the rear of a building, and upon investigation found Gibson beating his wife. The negro resisted arrest, and in the scuffle which followed, Gibson, who was powerfully built, threw Policeman Belding to the ground and took his club from him.
Belding drew his pistol and fired, the bullet hitting the negro just above the right ear and causing instant death.
The coroner's jury held that the killing was justifiable.

Newport, August, 17.—Light battery C of the Seventh regiment will leave Fort Adams today for San Francisco. They will soon embark for service in China.

MISSOURI EDITORS OUTING.

St. Louis, Aug. 17.—The annual session of the Missouri Press association opened at the Laclede hotel here today. Type setting machines, which are now in use in about ten of the county newspaper offices in the state, is the chief subject of discussion. The association will leave here after the adjournment tomorrow on an excursion for Niagara Falls and Quebec.

NEGRO MAN KILLED. Refused to Give the Road to White Texans. REPUBLIC SPECIAL. Austin, Tex., Aug. 17.—Information was received at the Executive Office this morning of the killing of a negro man by two white men near Rosanky, Tex., late yesterday afternoon. It is feared trouble will follow among the negroes in that section. The report received here states that while Charley Tolbert, a negro, with his wife and child, was driving near that place on the county road they were met by two white men, who demanded that they be given the road, as the side road was very muddy and as the two men were on horseback. Tolbert declined, whereupon the two began beating him over the head. Tolbert's wife begged for mercy for her husband, whereupon the two men drew their revolvers and shot Tolbert dead, after which they rode away. The men are unknown. Vienna Prominent Citizen Dead. REPUBLIC SPECIAL. Vienna, Mo., Aug. 17.—Doctor S. A. Gremp, aged 41 years, died at his home in this place this morning of consumption. He was one of the most prominent citizens of this county, being highly respected by every one. He was always first in every public enterprise and his death will be a great loss to the town and county. **
WILLIAM R. PAINTER,

THIS IN OHIO
Negro Boy Driven Out of Town Because He Is a Negro.
A negro boy named Walter Bryant, who drifted into the rockbound democratic suburb of Reading, Ohio, a few days ago, was given the most violent scare of his life Thursday night, August 23rd, when a crowd of about forty seized him and, after convincing him that he would be lynched if he ever returned to town, chased him out on the double quick. Reading citizens do not allow negroes in their town.

It was about 8 o'clock when he saw the mob at his door and heard cries of "Hang him!" String him up!"

Several men rushed in, seized him, slipped his head into a noose and he was dragged outside. He escaped and jumped into an apple barrel. He was caught again and tied to a tree. He cried, prayed and hysterically begged to be spared.

The crowd finally escorted him to the town limits and gave him a warning not to show his face in Reading again. He ran down the road like a deer.—New York World.
